paragraphs.heading: A worm beside deep-sea vents
paragraphs.text: The giant tubeworm, Riftia pachyptila, is a worm that lives in the deep sea beside hydrothermal vents. It stays fixed in one place, and many worms crowd together in big colonies around vents on the East Pacific Rise and the Galapagos Rift. A patch of them can stretch for tens of metres, and a single worm can grow to 3 m long. People first came across it in 1977, on an expedition to vents on the floor of the Galápagos Rift.

paragraphs.heading: A body with no gut
paragraphs.text: An adult has no mouth, no digestive system and no anus, and it does not eat. Its body is wormlike and makes a tube of chitin around itself for protection and support. At the front end is a red, feather-like plume, and the red comes from hemoglobin. Below the plume is a muscular region that holds the heart and the brain. The middle of the body holds the trophosome, a spongy tissue where bacteria live. The rear part anchors the worm to its tube.

paragraphs.heading: Fed by its bacteria
paragraphs.text: In place of eating, the worm depends on the bacteria in its trophosome for nutrition. The vents release large amounts of chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide, and the worm uses these for the bacteria's chemosynthesis. Hemoglobins in the plume bind O₂ and H₂S, which then travel through capillaries in the plume to the trophosome, where the bacteria can absorb them. The bacteria live inside special cells and have no contact with the outside environment. They depend completely on the worm to supply their nutrients and to take away their waste.

paragraphs.heading: Coping with harmful chemicals
paragraphs.text: Vents create low-oxygen conditions, and in such conditions organisms that store sulfur begin to make hydrogen sulfide (H₂S). In this worm that starts after 24 hours of low oxygen. H₂S can damage some body processes. The worm avoids the damage by binding H₂S to the haemoglobin in its blood and expelling it into its surroundings. Its hemoglobins are also unusual, since they can carry oxygen while sulfide is present without being blocked by it.

paragraphs.heading: Fast growth in the deep
paragraphs.text: This worm grows faster than any other known marine invertebrate. It has been known to settle a new site, become sexually mature and reach 1.5 m in length in under two years. Its tube grows by 10 to 85 cm a year. Deep-sea species that do not live at vents typically have low metabolic rates. In this worm, some enzyme activity is similar to that of shallow-living animals, which suggests a much faster metabolism than is usual for deep-sea animals.

paragraphs.heading: The tube
paragraphs.text: The tube is a cylinder, flexible and closed at the rear end. It can reach 2 m long and 5 cm across, and it is very thick next to the tubes of other tubeworms. It strongly resists attack by bacterial enzymes and can take years to decompose. If the worm senses a threat or is touched, it pulls its plume back into the tube. A worm can also adjust the top and the base of its tube, which gives it some room to adapt in a crowded colony.
